utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Salvatore Cannata, April Carter, Carmela Javier, and Dan Saxon for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Good day to everyone. Mr. Perisic is represented by Milos Androvic; Tina Drolec; our case manager, Daniela Tasic; Gregor Guy-Smith; and Novak Lukic as Defence counsel. THE COURT: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good morning, Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you, sir, that you made a declaration at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration. Thank you so much. Mr. Saxon, yesterday when we adjourned we were in private session. I don't know whether you still want to continue in private session. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the time being we can remain in open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are in open session. We'll stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering, with the Registrar's assistance, could we please see 65 ter 1279. And perhaps if we could initially make the top half of the B/C/S version a bit bigger for the convenience of General Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, if you take a look at the document that is on the screen in front of you, you'll see that it is from the -- or addressed to the Drina Corps Command -- excuse me, from the Drina Corps Command, strictly confidential number 19/14-471. It's dated 24 October 1993. And perhaps you could help us just for clarity, the heading on the upper left-hand corner, Drina Corps Command, is that the addressee of the document, or is that where the document is coming from?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the body that the document is coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it is said, first of all, the document is to be delivered to a number of brigades; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it refers to a telegram in the second paragraph dated the 23rd of October, 1993, from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska containing an order of the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Do you see that in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not getting any English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the large next paragraph describes how during the war, besides regular supplying of units and commands of the VRS based on the scheme of logistic support, there have appeared parallel chains of supplying of units in which besides authorised persons, various suppliers, donators, et cetera, have gotten involved. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following what you've been reading out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then it continues: "Such a way of supplying of commands and units have caused the uncontrolled, unplanned, and unappropriated outflow of all kinds of materiel, technical and other supplies from the VJ, even into the hands of the enemy, while at the same time it has caused enormous enrichment of individuals, justifiably causing deep dissatisfaction among the members of the VJ and the VRS." And then below that, we see that there is an order. It says: "Based on the jointly taken position and the agreement of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the commander of the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska ..." it says, "I order ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see at the bottom, the order is coming from General Ratko Mladic, the commander. And if we look at subparagraph 1 of the order, it reads: "In the future, the command of the units and organs will consolidate and submit to the General Staff of the VRS logistics sector all requests for the excerption of any kind of materiel supplies from the VJ." And then subparagraph 2, the order directs that: "Based on the requests that the command and units receive, the logistics sector of the GS VRS" - I believe that's' General Staff - "will carry out compilation of all the requests in accordance to branches and services three times a month, send requests to them for a signature, and then forward them to the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia for approval." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then it says: "Upon the approval of submitted requests obtained by the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, the logistics sector of the General Staff of the VJ, through its logistics bases, will organise excerption and distribution of approved items to units and organs, which is to be followed by proper materiel-bookkeeping documentation." That's subparagraph 3. And it says: "Neither one request will be considered or approved" - subparagraph 4 - "without my personal signature, the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ and his subordinated command." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And finally, subparagraph 5: "In the future, none of the commands and organs of the VJ will be in charge of approving or issuing any kind of materiel supplies from the VJ army fund without the approval and signature of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ." My question at this moment is, up to this point from what we've read, this order, the procedure outlined in this order from General Mladic, does it accord with the procedure that you were familiar with when you were addressing these kinds of requests for assistance from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm completely unfamiliar with the organisational structure of the VRS. I wasn't there, and I'm not familiar with the contents and the problems with this document. But what you are asking me about has to do with their internal organisation that, the procedure followed when obtaining requests, when receiving requests for supplies. This was probably a matter of an agreement between two states, two armies, but I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could leave this document, then, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean "leave"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not going to seek to tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P629 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to correct the transcript. When the answer was provided by the witness on page 15, the transcript, line 5, says: "Not every unit can contact the Chief of the General Staff directly." Whereas the witness says, Even in ours -- even in our staff, so the witness was making a distinction. He said not a single unit could contact the General Staff directly, not even our one. That's what the witness said, and it's not contained in the transcript. I think it's important. We can listen to the recording if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I see at line 5 is that: "Not every unit can contacts the Chief of the General Staff directly. This is the rule that has to be followed. This is the chain of command that has to be respected, and all armies throughout the world respect these rules." Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after this sentence -- yes, that's correct. After the word "... the General Staff directly ..." he added: Even our one, even our staff. And that isn't in the transcript. We could clear this up with the witness, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say. However, one word was omitted. I said, and I repeat, that no unit can contact directly the Chief of the General Staff, and that was also true of our army, of our General Staff, and of course that nobody from another army can contact our Chief of Staff. That would be unheard of. So this is a bit lengthier explanation of what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when you say nobody, you mean nobody in a lower rank unit, but the chief of the VRS can contact the General Staff of the VJ, can't it? That's the arrangement as we understand it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you for the clarification, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Mihajlovic, during 1994 and 1995, can you recall, was there ever an occasion when the VRS requested that the VJ provide it with mines?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall if you ever recommended that these requests for mines be approved?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every request was taken under advisement, and in keeping with the possibilities of our army, as I said yesterday, what happened most often was that those requests were corrected. The quantities were reduced, as I told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately how many mines the VJ provided to the VRS during 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot provide you with correct data. I don't have any records on me. The records did exist in the logistics sector. However, the total number of all kinds of mines as far as I can remember was about 100.000, and I'm talking about anti-tank mines, anti-personnel mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could ask Madam Registrar how much time I have taken up until now, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, are you able to help? 2 hours, 43 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we see document 65 ter 7901, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this is a document from the General Staff of the VJ. We see below that the word "sector," and then some abbreviations. Can you read that line to us, please, or do you know what those abbreviations stand for?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sector for air force and anti-aircraft defence, the aviation administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the document is dated the 4th of August, 1995. And then we see below that "to be delivered to ..." and several lines there with some abbreviations. Can you tell us what -- the first line begins with the number 608. Can you tell what that line says, what the abbreviations mean?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 608th logistics base of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And below that, the next line?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of air force and anti-aircraft defence. Further on, General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for information, and the last line is cabinet of the chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And reading below that says: "On the basis of a request from the VRS Main Staff" - Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska" - "dated the previous day" - 3rd of August, 1995 - "we agree that the following ..." and then there's another abbreviation. Can you tell us what that abbreviation means?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it means. This has to do with aviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And after that abbreviation, it says: "Be seated for the needs of the GS VRS." Below that, there is a list with four lines, also with abbreviations HN-42, HN-45, et cetera. Can you tell us what those abbreviations mean?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know what this is about, which equipment or materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Below that, it says that: "The 608th logistics base of the General Staff of the VJ will issue a ruling on the session of the mentioned materiel while the RV-PVO command will regulate the transfer to representatives of the General Staff" -- "Main Staff of the VRS." General, what was the role or function of the 608th Logistics Base of the General Staff of the VJ in this process, providing assistance to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 608th Logistics Base was the executive organ of the army and the ultimate organ that implemented all the previous requests; i.e., whatever we had agreed and ordered, they would put into force. They were the executive organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P630.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to say again, Mr. Saxon, I don't mean to interfere in -- you know, the guide-lines do say, once you have read through a document, particularly a short document like this, the preference is that it not be tendered because then you're burdening the record unnecessarily. You remember that? So if you do want to tender it, don't read it. The witness can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's something else if you are dealing with an illiterate witness, but this witness is highly educated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the term "combat readiness" as it was used in the JNA and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Combat readiness applies to the readiness of the troops for combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you be a little bit more specific. What does the concept entail or contain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Didn't the witness tell us this yesterday from the point of view of the engineering department where he works -- where he worked?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Point taken, Your Honour. I will move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the war between 1993 and 1995, were reports about the combat readiness of the VJ prepared?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports about the combat readiness of the VJ were prepared every year regularly, whereas the situation is monitored almost every day. Reports are drafted once a year at the end of the year or the beginning of next year for the previous year, and those reports cover all levels from the lowest unit level to the overall combat readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who would produce the final compilation of the combat readiness report for the VJ at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was -- that was within the jurisdiction of the sector for operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were -- was the combat readiness of the VJ reviewed at other times of the year in addition to this annual review at the end of each year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Control is part of the activities of the army at all levels. Superior Commands control the subordinated units, and at the highest level there was also the so-called inspection of combat readiness. That was the highest level of control which submitted reports to the Chief of the General Staff about the situation in the units that came under inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, why would it be necessary during the war years, 1993 to 1995, for the combat readiness of the VJ to be reviewed more than once a year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was an activity that had been done before any wars started, in peacetime. It's just part of the process of work in the army, and especially in the times of war around our borders, there was an additional reason for the state of combat readiness to be reviewed and monitored more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Your Honour, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I start my cross-examination, I would like to point to a mistake in the transcript. I did not want to interrupt my learned friend. I believe that it was just an omission. Can we go back to page 4, line 23, where Mr. Saxon quoted from the document that he eventually withdrew, so the document was not filed. Just a quote remains, but when he quoted, I believe that he made a mistake, but that mistake is relevant. This is the document, 65 ter 1279 that was not tendered for admission eventually. Mr. Saxon on page 4, and I quote, read item 3 of the order. I'm going to read very slowly in B/C/S, and you will see why this mistake appeared on line 24. This order under item 3 says as follows: "Upon the execution of the" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the text in front of them, and it is impossible to translate without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters. I would kindly ask for the document to be placed on the document, and I will read slowly. "When the requests were executed and approved by the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the logistics sector of the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska will via logistics bases organise the issuance and distribution of all the approved materiel and equipment to the units and institutions, and this will be accompanied by all the prescribed accountancy documents."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But let me say there was an English translation of this, wasn't there? I remember reading the English, and I think what is quoted here by Mr. Saxon is exactly as it stood in the English translation. Now, if you are saying that translation is wrong, then that translation needs to go and be corrected, but then it doesn't become necessary because that document was not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Absolutely right, Your Honours. However, I checked the English translation, and this logistics sector of the General Staff of the VRS is really something that exists in the document. However, what Mr. Saxon quoted on page 4, and I'm quoting from the transcript, I just wanted to correct the transcript and point out that there was a mistake made during Mr. Saxon's reading from the document. That was the point that I was making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. There it is on the screen, paragraph 3. Show us any reference to the Main Staff of the VRS there, in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the English version be moved just a little, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want you to show -- okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the second page. I can't see the item 3 in its entirety. I can't see number 3 in the English version. Can this be moved, please, so that I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not going to be able to see all of it at the same time. It will have to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I see. You can see that in the B/C/S version, the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska is mentioned, and I can't see this in the English version, in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, sir. I understand that. All I'm saying is Mr. Saxon did not misquote. The translation was incorrect if VRS is referred to. So this paragraph at page 4, line 23 is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are absolutely right. Mr. Saxon was reading from the English version, and I did not intervene. I should have because there's obviously a discrepancy between the B/C/S original and the English translation, which I am aware of now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, do you have anything to suggest about that situation? I don't know what you -- before I ask you, what do you want us to do about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to read the authentic part from the B/C/S document because this was not recorded. It is not a correction of the transcript because Mr. Saxon was reading properly what is written in the translation. This is now just my intervention with regard to the translation, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much then, Mr. Lukic. Thank you for that intervention. You may proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, sir, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to examine you on behalf of General Perisic Defence, and before I start doing that, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the two of us speak the same language, but you have realised how long it takes interpreters to interpret our words. That's why I'm going to ask you to slow down and also to make a little pause after each of my questions to allow the interpreters to interpret the question. Also, I will make a little pause after your answer before I start putting my next question. Yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, General, you spoke about the structure of the General Staff, and you mentioned two terms which are very important for me, and I believe that it is important to use them properly when they are translated into English. You mentioned a term "branches and services." Could you please tell us what branches of the army are?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branches of the army are the land army, the air force, and the anti-aircraft defence, and the navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as for the services, there are also branches. For example, in the land forces there is infantry; there is artillery; there is -- are more than mechanised units; there are engineers; and there's also a BHO, which stands for atomic, biological, and chemical defence. As for the other services, I may be wrong, and I don't want to do that. And there are also the so-called services or sectors in the logistics. For example, there's quartermaster service, technical service, traffic, medical service. There's also veterinary service. I may have skipped one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted you to clarify certain terms, and now I will move on to the engineers. The chief of the administration of engineers is actually the highest professional management and supervision organ of that service; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, there are two other terms or, rather, one term that you mentioned, and I would like you to explain the two to us layperson. There are administrations and independent administrations. So what are we talking about? Which are the independent administrations in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration of certain branches or services were part of the combat arms; like, for example, when we are talking about land army, my administration was subordinated to the chief of sector for the land army who was also the assistant of the chief of General Staff for the land army. And there were also several independent administrations which were directly subordinated to the Chief of the General Staff. For example, there was the administration for morale, the intelligence administration, the security administration, and I don't know whether there were any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And again from the layman perspective, the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff were -- its members were chiefs of sectors and chiefs of independent administrations; am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the army commanders, did they attend the collegium meetings regularly or were they invited?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they would attend meetings occasionally, not regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff dealt with some regular topics at each meeting and there are some special topics that were put on the agenda as needed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I tried to explain yesterday. There are some regular topics from the purview of the elements of the combat readiness of the military. There's also the intelligence and security situation, the situation in the units, issues and problems with replenishment training, everything that had to do with the regular life of the army. There was also the topic of extraordinary events, which comprised disasters and accidents. Also, there are personnel issues that were put on the agenda occasionally when people were promoted into higher ranks, the training of the staff in higher education institutions, and that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think we could have a break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just before the break, General, I put a question about the work of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff with regard to subjects discussed at those meetings. My question is as follows: Would you agree with me if I said that the Chief of the Main Staff at those collegiums put certain questions to his associates who were members of the collegium; he listened to their suggestions and he asked for their opinions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I assume that at the end of the collegium, once he had been provided with all the necessary information, he would then assign tasks. He would take decisions and do everything else that he had the authority to do as the Chief of the General Staff; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your personal experience, did Mr. Perisic respect the suggestions of the members of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff? Did he abide by the decisions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally have a very positive experience of that, although I wasn't a regular member at those collegiums, but occasionally I had the opportunity to personally address or respond to an invitation from him to deal with certain tasks within the domain of my service. This usually concerned a request to carry out work for the needs of the civilian population. He accept all my suggestions. He accepted all my suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were the deputy chief of the engineering administration before 1993. I apologise, perhaps you said this yesterday, but when did you have that position of the deputy chief?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1991. That's when I assumed that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was when the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we are interested in 1992 and 1993 when the war in Bosnia started, so before you became the chief, you were the deputy chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, the Chief of the Main Staff was Zivota Panic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to pause after having put his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you have to pause briefly after I have put my question to you, and I have to pause too. The interpreters have just warned us to do this.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday - I'm speaking about the year 1991 and 1992 - you said that the economic situation in the country was very difficult, and before this Court we have heard evidence according to which from 1993 until the end of the year inflation had run amuck. There was hyperinflation and the entire economy of the -- of Yugoslavia was functioning very poorly. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These were the reasons for the poor logistic situation of the Army of Yugoslavia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, therefore, it was also the reason for why they were poorly equipped with materiel and equipment, had to do with military and industry; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of consumption, but production was not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that before Mr. Perisic became the Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the situation with regard to the reserves, the materiel and equipment, was very poor in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was in a poor situation even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that before he assumed the position of the Chief of the Main Staff, the aid sent to the VRS wasn't institutionalised? When I say that, it means that you didn't submit a request through the Main Staff of the VRS to the office of the Chief of the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure how this worked at the time. All I know is that later, order of some kind was established. I personally even during the previous period didn't have any direct contact, but I don't know what the case was with regard to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you didn't have direct contact, but did you hear about situations in the previous period according to which units from the VRS or individuals directly contacted units or institutions of the Army of Yugoslavia? Did this occur on a lower, so to speak, horizontal level without any supervision, without any control?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you agree that the legal obligations of the Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia was to ensure that the army was put to good use and that included materiel and equipment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's his responsibility for the overall situation in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Above all, that is in order to carry out the army's main task, to secure the state borders and the state territory?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and to be in a state of combat readiness if it's necessary to defend the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you told Mr. Saxon when you discussed the subject of combat readiness. Would you agree with me if I said that when establishing such a relationship, well, the Chief of the General Staff has to agree to certain proposals from subordinate units and institutions, and this is in order to have an overall view of the situation with regard to the materiel and equipment that the Army of Yugoslavia has at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear to me. Every lower level organ is also responsible for the overall situation, for the personnel, for the situation with regard to personnel and materiel. The Chief of the General Staff is responsible for these matters, but he can't be aware of the situation in all the relevant areas, in all the areas which result in a certain degree of combat readiness in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I assume that you are familiar with the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia. You're not a lawyer, but you certainly know that the supreme commander of the Army of Yugoslavia was the President of the republic in accordance with the law in force on the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's the President of the republic or the Supreme Defence Council. I'm not sure which period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very briefly, I'd like to have the following called up on the screen: P197, page 1. This is the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, Article 4. We'll go through it very briefly. I'm interested in the first two paragraphs in Article 4. We'll wait for the English version to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or could you zoom in in large Article 4. I'll read through it very slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness asked which period you are referring to, so you've got to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm asking you about relates to the time when Mr. Perisic was appointed as the Chief of the Main Staff, from the end of 1993 onwards. That's when he held this position.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Article 4, it states the following: "The President of the republic shall command the army in war and in peace in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, and then in his command of the army, the President of the republic shall, 1, establish the principles of internal organisation, the development and equipping of the army." You've already commented on the law. We'll now interpret who is responsible for what. Do you remember, General, that Momcilo Perisic at the collegiums of the General staff informed the members of the decisions and orders issued by the President of the republic in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Council?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't present at such meetings. I wasn't a regular member of the collegium, as I have said. Some information was relayed, I remember that, but I can't remember the content of the information relayed. I knew what was at stake, but I wasn't sure -- because of the time that has passed, I wasn't sure whether it was the President of the republic or whether the supreme council that was responsible, but now it's clear to me having seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. General, in the course of your work, did you ever come across a case in which General Perisic in which the Chief of the General Staff the Army of Yugoslavia requested that something should be done by bypassing the procedure that you have been referring to? You mentioned a procedure when it comes to providing materiel assistance, technical assistance. You said this was done through requests from the Chief of the Main Staff, and one would also have to obtain the opinion of the relevant administration, for example, your administration. Did you ever hear about Mr. Perisic authorizing some equipment to be provided without asking for your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me be broader. In general, when it was necessary to follow certain procedure and to ask for an administration's opinion, were there any cases in which Perisic acted willfully or on his own initiative and failed to respect the procedure that had to be followed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, I wasn't the only one who participated in that procedure. There were other colleagues of mine from other administrations who were involved in the procedure. Often, we worked together. Everyone was responsible for his own field. They were responsible for ammunition, tank shells. I was responsible for ordinance, explosives. So this procedure concerned all of us. I know who I worked with, and that's how things worked. As for whether there were any exceptions, well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have document P621 MFI on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You answered questions put to you about this document by Mr. Saxon yesterday, and now you say that you can't remember any cases in which the procedure that you have mentioned wasn't followed. Can I therefore conclude that there was a request from the Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia to act in this way? You then acted in accordance with this request from the Chief of the Main Staff to provide ammunition, for example.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday I said that there was something missing here, another document. That's the request from the General Staff of Republika Srpska. It should have contained someone's position, the chief's position, the sector's position. It depended on how I obtained the document. I couldn't do this on my own initiative, but when copying documents -- well, I don't understand why this other document doesn't exist along with this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say copying documents, you mean what was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy of that document of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P624 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, also, you discussed this document. You commented on the document yesterday. You commented on the handwritten part at the top, "give it to Ratko to have this solved"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this look like the handwriting of the Chief of the Main Staff? Now -- well, could we have a look at the second page of the document now. Could we have a look at the bottom, in the lower part of the document, as you can see. We're interested in the bottom part of the document. Thank you. We have a signature from the office of the Chief of the Main Staff. We have a number and date, and that's to the left; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then we have the text that was read out to you yesterday, and it was signed on behalf of the chief of the office by Colonel Borovic. This was sent to the logistics sector, to the -- to Mr. Milovanovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: His name was Ratko; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ratko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that he is deceased?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see that the Chief of the Main Staff in the written part of the text said, "give it to Ratko..." He had Ratko Milovanovic in mind. He was in the sector for logistics of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if there are certain requests sent from the Main Staff of the VRS, as I understand it when the Chief of the General Staff or his office received the request, he asks Ratko Milovanovic the logistics sector to check to see whether this equipment can be provided; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the responsibility of that sector is. Whatever isn't the responsibility of the sector is then forwarded to other sectors that are responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then they provide their opinions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They provide their opinions, and it's sent back to the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's how I understood this document. You can't see in this document whether this request was met, whether anything was provided, everything or whether the procedure was launched and whether an inquiry would be made into whether something could be provided pursuant to the request; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I am reading this document. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, General, that when there was a need for certain -- okay, the first question: When it comes to mines and other technical means that were within the purview of your engineers administration, were such things produced by the military industry of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of that -- there were a lot of supplies left over from the period after the Second World War which had come from the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the Army of Yugoslavia could not directly take anything from the military industry of Yugoslavia without the approval and consent of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Ministry of Defence had organisation units that were responsible for supply and procurement. They were the main organ through which supplies were executed, and it all depended on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the military industry of Yugoslavia was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now you've just mentioned the division for procurement of the Ministry of Defence. Are you aware of the division of military and economic activities? Do you know what this division was in charge of? If you don't know, you just say so.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I never had any contacts with that division.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Radojica Kadijevic do you know what General Kadijevic did, where he was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know he was affiliated with the ministry, but I can't remember his position. He was dealing with the issues of production of the military industry. I don't know his function, his exact function.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I won't dwell upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise. You said that he was with the ministry. Did you mean the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I meant the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. And now let's go back to the procedure that was necessary to send the assistant to the Army of Republika Srpska. When you provided your opinion or recommendation or consent, when you said that it was possible to send a certain quantity of mines, for example, you wouldn't know whether that was provided or not. As far as I could understand you, this recommendation went to the logistics sector, and then the logistics sector had to find means and ways to distribute the requested equipment. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my consent, the consent of my administration, there would be a remark to be taken from the 1st Army, from the 2nd Army because we maintained records, and we were aware of the situation of replenishment, and we would suggest that the materiel and equipment be taken from where they were -- from where they were plentiful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean to be taken from where there was enough?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any feedback from, for example, the logistics base of the 1st Army that the means and equipment were sent? Were you provided with such information?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, if your administration, the engineers administration in the course of 1994 and 1995 maintained special records of the quantities of mines that were sent to the Army of Republika Srpska, for example?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We maintained records all the time. Even before, during the existence of the JNA, and later, all the time while I was a member of the army, the records were updated constantly. My desk officer would go to the technical administration twice a year. He would go to the logistics sector, and he would collate the records with the books maintained by the person in charge of the same thing in the logistics. That means that the chiefs of the army and not the subordinated unions would have yearly briefings on the combat activities of their branches; and in addition to other things, they would also inform on the quantities of the equipment and materiel that they had at their disposal. That was also one way of collate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you maintained records of how much was sent to the Army of Republika Srpska. I was not interested in the overall records.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, on our records we also maintained records of how much of what means and technical equipment were sent to one or the other army; for example, in the Republika Srpska or the Serbian Army of Krajina, yes, we did maintain such records as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's fine. It's not only you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters. Can we please move into private session just for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the Chamber please move into private session. 16 [Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I may have misspoken. And if we can go on in private session, I would like to discuss another document with the witness for which I would like us to be in private session. I don't know whether the document P623 MFI is also under seal or not. If it's not, then -- if it is, then we could remain. Just a moment. Could the document please be put on the screen for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke about this document yesterday. At the request of the Army Republika Srpska, there is a reference to some -- if the document to be lowered a little for the General to be able to see the signature. It is your signature, sir, and this is a request for anti-infantry mines; the total quantity is 10.000. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now scroll up a little. As far as I can see, the document was drafted in May 1995; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, General, if I say that anti-infantry and anti-tank mines are actually defensive devices that are intended to prevent the onslaught of the enemy; in my lay terms, I would explain that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are means of defence which is used to protect the positions and lines of the units that are defending a certain sector and certain positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Do you remember that during this period of time in May or, rather, in spring 1995, there was a major offensive launched by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in very large parts of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina against the Army of Republika Srpska, and that was already towards the end of the war, to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember having heard stories. I remember having seen and listened about that on the media. I know that this was going on, but I don't really remember during which period of time, but I believe your word. I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that this quantity of 10.000 mines was among the biggest deliveries that were allowed at the time, and I'm talking about the quantity.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. This was within the limits of the previous requests. There were even larger quantities before. This is a somewhat smaller quantity, I would say. Sometimes there were requests for 20.000, but as I've already told you we usually reduce these numbers. We would bring the numbers down very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's put aside the request. I'm talking about the quantity that was approved. Was this something out of the ordinary or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was approved, and it was nothing out of the ordinary, 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document can be removed from the screen, and we can go back into open session, but we will continue talking about this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Please bear with me. Can we look at your statement, the one that you provided to the OTP of this Tribunal on the 27th and 30th January, 2005. This is document 1D005965. Could this please be put on the screen, paragraph 17, page 9 in B/C/S version, and I hope the representative of the Registry will be able to assist me with the equivalent English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the number of 100.000 mines, and you say - and let me jog your memory, General - it says amongst other things in this paragraph 17 -- can we scroll down a little in B/C/S. Towards the end of this paragraph, you say: "On some five or six occasions, I recommended for the forces of the VRS at their request to be supplied with mines. In the course of these two years, a total of 100.000 different types of mines were provided to the VRS ..." You said that you remembered that there were five or six such cases. Is it possible that we are not talking about such a large number of 100.000? Maybe you supplied less mines.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is possible. It may have been less. There may have been more than this number of occasions. I saw some documents here which prove that there were requests in 1993 and approvals, as well, so I was not sure then, and I'm still not sure, but I don't think there were more mines than this figure. I confirmed to you that the records were maintained. I don't have the records on me, and I can't give you the exact quantities. There's no way for me to be sure of the exact quantity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said in this statement that according to your opinion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please make a break, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that in your opinion or according to what you knew, about 1 million mines have remained in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina once the JNA had left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember having mentioned that figure?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that that quantity of mines fell into the hands of all the three warring parties, but would you agree with me that most of the -- those mines ended up in the hands of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain quantity of mines and other explosives that had belonged to the units deployed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina were supplemented by some of the mines and explosives that were being pulled out from the republics of Slovenia and Croatia, and all that remained in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all that together, and I suppose that when we are talking about mines that a total figure of those mines were about 1 million, and they were taken over by the units of the three militaries that had been established in the meantime, the Serb military, the Muslim military, and the Croatian military. I don't know the ratio and how much each of the militaries took. I suppose that most of those mines ended up with the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, according to what you know, what was the relationship of the VRS towards that equipment? Did they use it rationally?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was war-time. The situations varied. When I had contact with colleagues, with associates, I heard that this equipment wasn't used very rationally. Certain areas would be mined. Mines would be laid, and then when the unit left, the mines wouldn't be taken away; they would be left there, or there were temporary warehouses from which they didn't take away the equipment because of ongoing fighting or for other reasons. And this is why I'm saying that I don't think that this equipment was used rationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. In any event, yesterday you said, and you've emphasised this today, given the requests of the VRS that you received -- well, not all the requests were granted. Only some of the requests were granted for the needs of the VRS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll now move on to another subject, but I'd just like to make use of this page of the transcript. Could we just scroll up a bit and see item 15 in the B/C/S version. It's your statement. Yesterday, Mr. Saxon asked you about the 30th centre, the 30th Personnel Centre. I'll read out part of your statement, and then I'll ask you whether you stand by what you said. I'm going to start in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph are you reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's paragraph 15 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from the mid-section.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "I believe that the 30th Personnel Centre was used to administer the personnel files and related paperwork of those VJ officers, the non-commissioned officers born in Bosnia who agreed to return to Bosnia and serve in the VRS. Most officers I believe answered the call-up of the 30th Personnel Centre and went to serve in Bosnia. However, I believe that some did not. Those who did not respond to the call-up didn't suffer any consequences. The 30th Personnel Centre also administered the officers and non-commissioned officers of the former JNA who remained in Bosnia after the conflict had erupted, and it also administered VJ personnel who were not born in Bosnia but voluntarily joined the VRS." General, could you just confirm that this is what you in fact said, and do you stand by that? Is that the information that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and according to what I know, I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's another subject I would like to deal with now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, what do you want to do with this statement on the screen? ID 005965?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't want this witness statement to be admitted. I just wanted to show parts of the document to the witness, so I don't want the entire document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we'll now go through another three documents, which will provide us with a clear picture on what you had been testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the document 7899, item 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is request from the Main Staff of the VRS dated the 26th of May, 1995, and I can see that it's addressed to your administration, to the engineers administration, and equipment is being requested. Are these things that your administration is generally responsible for, the things referred to here? Are these the categories of equipment that you would be responsible for?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at page 2 on the screen in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a telegram sent from the Main Staff signed by Ratko Mladic, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic. Under A and B, it says that the 14th POB, logistics base will take over the above-mentioned equipment. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know whose base.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you about. Do you know about there being a 14th POB in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I'm not familiar with their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we have a look at this, let's have a look at another document. 7899, item 3 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document, can I just ask the witness. I see -- I've been seeing this in quite a number of documents, like this English one, it's there also on the B/C/S, that a number of q's and a line at the bottom. Do those q's mean anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just see. Where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we can show the bottom of the B/C/S, well, if this is still the same document. See, on the English side below Ratko Mladic, there are a number of q's there. They are also there on the left side on the B/C/S, but there are fewer. Is this -- at the end of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that, but I don't know what this stands for. It must be a code from a teleprinter, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just correct the transcript, make a minor correction. With regard to the document, I wanted to show the transcript says that I asked for 7899, document 7899. I asked for 78099 [as interpreted], item 02. I asked to see -- I'll repeat the number. I asked to see document 07899, item 02.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This one that's on the screen, it has been tendered already through the Prosecution, or what do you want to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this document has been admitted into evidence. It's a similar document. I would like to tender it, but I wanted to have a look at all the three documents concerned and ask for each one to be admitted. There are three documents. It was on the list, the documents that the Prosecution wanted to show to the witness, and then Mr. Saxon decided not to do this. It would be best, perhaps, to request that it be admitted into evidence in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it could be under seal since there are still a state request. We agreed that this document should be given an MFI number, since it's part of the documents from the seventh additional Prosecution list, so perhaps it could retain the MFI number. In general, we won't be objecting to this document. We ourselves suggest that it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. You were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution agrees with Mr. Lukic's suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May 7899 then be admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D56 marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have the other document on the screen, 07899, item 03.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it item 03 or item 02?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 3 on the screen now. In the previous document, it was item 2. I'm told that we don't have an English translation of this document, Your Honours. I don't know whether I should read the entire document out or just read out a couple of sentences and wait for the translation. I just want the witness to confirm that this is his signature and that it has to do with the previous request. Perhaps I should read it out aloud so that you can follow, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead. Do what you want to do, but do give us a translation in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document, it has a stamp in which it says the General Staff -- the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the KOV sector, engineers administration, POV BR, confidential number 286/3-3, 30th of May, 1995. To the right, it says: Military secret, confidential; title: Providing engineering equipment, NVO --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can help us. And MES?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mines and ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: VRS, that's the Army of the Republika Srpska, authorisation forwarded to, and then it says to the office of the chief of the GS VJ; subject: Related to the document of the GS VRS, strictly confidential number 04/11-29, dated the 26th of May, 1995: "The engineers administration, which is responsible for engineering equipment such as NVO and MES, has reviewed the GS VRS request and hereby expresses its position with regard to the request. "Item 1. Regardless of the fact that there is a shortage of engineering equipment such as NVO and MES in the VJ, we agree to provide the GS VRS with the following equipment ..." I don't think it's necessary to read through all of these items here. I'll just read out item 2. A certain equipment is mentioned under that item. It says: "We are not in a position to provide the other equipment requested because of the critical situation." It's signed by the chief. Here it says Colonel Milan Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladen Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Mladen. General, you signed this document, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this document correspond to the previous request that we had a look at awhile ago?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it confirms what you testified about. When something was requested, you would examine the possibilities of the Army of Yugoslavia, and you would then express your position and say that some equipment should be provided or shouldn't be provided; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you would forward that to the office of the Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. That's your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we remove this document, without going through all that equipment that is listed there, can you tell us what type of equipment that is that is being supplied? In general terms, not each item.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 1 -- under item 1, requests are made for mechanical and other types of detonators for certain mines; then electrical detonators requested; yesterday, as we said, sort of a missile device was requested; a mining cable; engineering and sabotage equipment is requested; equipment for mining work; and then "asovcici" are requested. These are tools that enable soldiers to dig in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this admitted into evidence, please. [In English] Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence under seal, I thought -- and MFI'd. Is that what counsel said because I didn't hear that from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, may it please be given an exhibit number, marked for identification, under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D57 marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I'm calling for 65 ter 7897. Could this please be put on the screen. I'm sorry. It's on the screen already. I was looking at LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you see the document in front of you? This is a letter sent by the cabinet of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, am I right, which was sent to the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's not read the whole document, but let me ask you, do you agree with me that the contents of this document correspond with the position that you assent in the previous document to the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia? This is just a confirmation of what you wrote in the previous document; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by Colonel Sinisa Borovic. You know that at the time he was the chief of the cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know he was the chief of the cabinet, but I don't know during which period of time. Now I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this document actually confirms what you spoke about the entire procedure, starting with the request, providing the opinion, and then your opinion was sent to the Chief of the General Staff for his approval.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted into evidence. It doesn't have to be now. We can wait for the Prosecution to confirm that this document is not under seal, and until then I would like this document to be admitted as a public document without any restrictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why can't we admit it under seal now until we hear from the Prosecution? It is so admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D58 under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Any re-examination, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A few minutes, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move into private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually. I can do that in a moment. Perhaps if we can stay in public session and call up again Exhibit P197, which Mr. Lukic used with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could focus on Article 4, please, in the B/C/S version, as well, for the assistance of the ... General, you were shown the Law on the Army, this particular Exhibit, during cross-examination of my colleague Mr. Lukic, and your attention was directed to Article 4, which begins saying -- it gives the authority of the President vis-a-vis the army in the beginning, and then it says: "In his command of the army, the President of the republic shall ..." and then there's a list of items that the President is responsible for. And if you could, if we could focus --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S version, please. And if we could focus in on the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In subparagraph 8, the President is to perform other duties relating to the command over the army in accordance with -- I think that's federal law. I can't quite read it. If we could scroll to the left in the English version. Yes. And then the last sentence it says that in performing the duties --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see Article 8, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Really? Can we zoom in on Article 8 for the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's not Article -- I'm sorry. It's subparagraph 8, General. We're still in Article 4. We've just gone over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I understand now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And in the last part of the subparagraph 8, the President of the republic shall issue orders, commands, and decisions. Are you following with me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can follow. I can follow item 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I'm sorry we excused the witness in private session. We should have done it in open session. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Cannata will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I can have some time to just switch the computer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Your Honour, may Ms. Carter be excused from the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Carter is excused but not you. You didn't ask for yourself. Are you also asking to be excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I need to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, you are excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will remain in your company, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Dr. Milan Mandilovic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
